questions.q: State the ICMR 2020 RDA for energy (kcal/day) and protein (g/day) for a sedentary adult man and a sedentary adult woman (18–60 years). How does the protein RDA differ per kg body weight between genders?
questions.a: Sedentary adult man: 2110 kcal, 54 g protein (0.83 g/kg for 65 kg reference weight). Sedentary adult woman: 1660 kcal, 46 g protein (0.83 g/kg for 55 kg reference weight). Protein RDA per kg body weight is identical (0.83 g/kg) — the absolute difference arises from reference body weights. A wrong answer stating different g/kg values reveals confusion between absolute RDA and weight-normalised requirement; students often memorise absolute numbers without understanding the per-kg basis.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman shifts from a sedentary desk job to a moderate-activity job (standing, walking 4–5 hours daily). Her energy RDA increases by ~350 kcal. Explain why her *iron* RDA does NOT increase proportionally, while her *thiamine* RDA does.
questions.a: Iron RDA for adult women (18–50 y) is fixed at 19 mg/day (to cover menstrual losses) regardless of activity; it is not energy-linked. Thiamine RDA is set at 0.5 mg/1000 kcal — so when energy allowance rises, thiamine rises proportionally. A wrong answer claiming iron increases with activity shows misunderstanding of nutrient classification: iron is a "fixed physiological need" nutrient, thiamine is an "energy-linked" nutrient. This distinction is critical for board case-study questions.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male marketing executive travels 4 days/week, eats restaurant meals high in sodium and saturated fat, sleeps 6 hours, and drinks 3–4 alcoholic drinks on travel days. His lipid profile shows LDL 160 mg/dL, HDL 35 mg/dL, triglycerides 220 mg/dL. Using ICMR RDA as baseline, specify *three* quantitative dietary modifications (with target values) you would prescribe, justifying each with the lifestyle factor it addresses.
questions.a: (1) Sodium ≤ 2000 mg/day (vs. RDA 2000 mg) — addresses restaurant meals; further restriction to 1500 mg if hypertensive. (2) Saturated fat < 7% of total energy (vs. RDA < 10%) — addresses alcohol + high-fat meals raising LDL. (3) Omega-3 (EPA+DHA) 250–500 mg/day — counters triglyceride elevation from alcohol and refined carbs. A wrong answer giving only qualitative advice ("eat less salt") fails the board's competency requirement for *quantitative* prescription with ICMR-referenced targets.

questions.q: Compare the *magnitude* of increase in energy RDA from sedentary to heavy activity for adult men vs. women. Then analyse why the *percentage* increase is similar (~55%) despite different absolute increments.
questions.a: Men: 2110 → 3470 kcal (+1360 kcal, +64%). Women: 1660 → 2720 kcal (+1060 kcal, +64%). The percentage is similar because ICMR scales energy RDA by *reference body weight* and *PAL (Physical Activity Level)* multipliers, which are gender-neutral. Absolute increments differ due to higher male reference weight (65 vs 55 kg). A wrong answer stating "men need more because they are bigger" without referencing the PAL-based calculation method misses the mechanistic link tested in JEE-style analytical questions.

questions.q: Critique this meal plan for a sedentary adult woman (1660 kcal RDA): Breakfast — 2 aloo parathas with butter (450 kcal), Lunch — white rice 200g, rajma 100g, curd 100g (550 kcal), Evening — samosa + chai with sugar (350 kcal), Dinner — 3 rotis, paneer butter masala 150g, salad (600 kcal). Total ~1950 kcal. Identify *three* specific nutrient gaps relative to RDA that *persist even if calories are reduced to 1660 kcal by portion control*.
questions.a: (1) Dietary fibre ~15 g (RDA 25 g) — refined flour parathas, white rice, no whole grains/vegetables. (2) Calcium ~400 mg (RDA 1000 mg) — only curd and paneer provide dairy; volume insufficient. (3) Vitamin C ~20 mg (RDA 55 mg) — no citrus, amla, guava, capsicum; cooking destroys vitamin C in rajma. A wrong answer focusing only on "excess calories" misses that *micronutrient density* is independent of energy adjustment — a key board exam concept.

questions.q: Design a one-day menu for a 28-year-old female night-shift nurse (moderate activity, 2110 kcal RDA) who sleeps 7 am–2 pm, works 8 pm–8 am. The menu must: (a) distribute protein evenly across 4 eating occasions (≥20 g each), (b) include ≥400 mg calcium in the pre-shift meal, (c) limit caffeine to ≤200 mg post-midnight, (d) provide ≥500 mg potassium in the post-shift recovery meal. Specify foods with weights.
questions.a: Pre-shift (6:30 pm): 150g curd + 50g roasted chana + 100g banana + 2 ragi rotis (protein 22g, Ca 420mg, K 800mg). During shift (10 pm): 100g paneer bhurji + 2 multigrain rotis + 100g apple (protein 24g, Ca 300mg). Post-midnight (2 am): 1 cup green tea (30mg caffeine) + 30g almonds (protein 6g, K 200mg). Post-shift recovery (8:30 am): 100g soy nuggets pulao (brown rice 80g + veg) + 150g curd + 100g orange (protein 28g, K 900mg, Ca 350mg). Total protein ~80g (1.45 g/kg), Ca ~1370mg, caffeine 30mg. A poor answer clusters protein in one meal or ignores circadian nutrient timing — tested in CUET case studies.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Adult nutrition refers to the dietary requirements and recommended dietary allowances (RDAs) for men and women aged 18–60 years, accounting for gender-specific ______ needs, activity levels, and lifestyle factors such as occupation, physical activity, stress, sleep patterns, and substance use that modify nutrient needs for optimal health and disease prevention.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a dietitian consulting a 35-year-old male ______ engineer who works night shifts, sleeps 5 hours, drinks alcohol twice a week, and does no exercise — his BMI is 28.
What is Adult nutrition? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Adult nutrition refers to the dietary requirements and recommended dietary allowances (RDAs) for men and women aged 18–60 years, accounting for gender-specific physiological needs, activity levels, and lifestyle factors such as occupation, physical activity, stress, sleep patterns, and substance use that modify nutrient needs for optimal.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) interpret ICMR RDA tables to determine energy, protein, fat, vitamin, and mineral requirements for adult men and women across sedentary, moderate, and heavy activity categories; (2) explain how specific lifestyle factors (shift work, chronic stress, alcohol, smoking, sedentary behaviour) alter nutrient.
